content: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a significant global public health issue, responsible for approximately 399,000 deaths annually, primarily due to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In 2019, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimated that 58 million people were living with chronic HCV infection, with the majority of the burden concentrated in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Around 5 million new HCV infections occur each year, predominantly through injecting drug use, sexual transmission (especially among men who have sex with men), and unsafe healthcare practices. HCV infection is caused by six major genotypes, with their distribution varying by geographic region. In May 2016, the 69th World Health Assembly endorsed the Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS) for 2016–2021, aiming to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. Elimination is defined as a 90% reduction in new chronic infections and a 65% reduction in mortality compared to 2015 levels. Achieving these targets requires scaling up prevention, testing, and treatment interventions to diagnose 90% of those infected and treat 80% of those diagnosed. As of 2019, only 21% of the 58 million people with HCV infection had been diagnosed, and just 13% had received treatment. HCV infection can cause both acute and chronic hepatitis. Approximately 20% of individuals with acute infection experience early symptoms, and about 25% clear the virus spontaneously within six months without treatment. However, 55–85% of cases progress to chronic infection, which can lead to progressive liver fibrosis and cirrhosis. The risk of developing cirrhosis in chronic HCV infection ranges from 15% to 30% after 20 years. Initially, cirrhosis is compensated, but it may progress to decompensated cirrhosis, resulting in complications such as variceal hemorrhages, ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, encephalopathy, and renal impairment. Annually, 1–3% of individuals with cirrhosis develop HCC. Factors such as age at infection, alcohol use, HBV or HIV coinfection, and immunosuppression increase the risk of cirrhosis and HCC. HIV coinfection, particularly in individuals with advanced immunodeficiency, accelerates progression to cirrhosis and HCC. HCV infection is also associated with extrahepatic manifestations, including depression (24%), diabetes mellitus (15%), and chronic kidney disease (10%). Immune-related conditions, such as mixed cryoglobulinemia, B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), are less common but directly attributable to HCV infection. These extrahepatic manifestations often improve with treatment and are generally independent of liver fibrosis severity. In 2010, an estimated 5% of healthcare injections were administered with reused, unsterilized devices, leading to 315,000 new HCV infections annually. Addressing this issue requires safer healthcare practices, the introduction of reuse-prevention injection devices, and reducing unnecessary injections. Globally, injecting drug use accounts for 23% of new HCV infections, and 8% of current infections occur among people who inject drugs. This population faces increased all-cause mortality due to the combined effects of drug use, socioeconomic challenges, limited healthcare access, and environmental factors. Other transmission routes include mother-to-child transmission (8–25% in HIV/HCV coinfected women), tattooing, body piercing, and needlestick injuries in healthcare workers. Sexual transmission is infrequent in heterosexual couples but more common among men who have sex with men, particularly those who are HIV-negative. Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) have revolutionized HCV treatment, offering high efficacy across all six major genotypes. Pangenotypic DAAs, such as sofosbuvir/velpatasvir and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, simplify treatment by eliminating the need for genotyping, streamlining procurement, and expanding global access. Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir is effective against genotypes 1–6, including HIV/HCV coinfection and compensated or decompensated cirrhosis. Sofosbuvir/daclatasvir is another effective combination, particularly for genotypes 1–4, but may be less effective against certain subtypes endemic in sub-Saharan Africa. Access to DAAs was initially limited by high costs, but the availability of low-cost generic medicines has improved access, particularly in LMICs. WHO guidelines have been updated to include recommendations for DAA use in children aged three years and older, simplified service delivery models, and point-of-care HCV RNA testing for diagnosis and cure confirmation. These updates align with WHO’s modular approach to guideline development, incorporating emerging evidence to improve HCV prevention, testing, care, and treatment. The WHO guideline development process involved a multidisciplinary steering committee and a Guidelines Development Group, ensuring representation from diverse stakeholders, including patient advocacy groups, researchers, and clinicians. Systematic reviews, meta-analyses, cost-effectiveness analyses, and surveys informed the recommendations, with a focus on outcomes important to patients. The GRADE framework was used to assess the certainty of evidence and the strength of recommendations, which were classified as either strong or conditional based on the balance of benefits and harms, evidence certainty, and stakeholder values. In summary, eliminating HCV as a public health threat by 2030 requires addressing gaps in diagnosis and treatment, expanding access to affordable DAAs, and implementing effective prevention strategies. Continued efforts to simplify care delivery, integrate services, and prioritize vulnerable populations are essential to achieving global elimination targets.
